dmm-2007-power-01.title: Example
dmm-2007-power-01.body: $r(x)=x+\frac12$: for an integer $z$, $r(z)=z+\frac12$ is a half-integer, never an integer.

dmm-2007-power-02.title: Ordered selections
dmm-2007-power-02.body: Choose the $n$ members in order: $z$ choices for the first, $z-1$ for the second, ..., $z-n+1$ for the $n$th: $z(z-1)\cdots(z-n+1)$ ordered selections. Each subcommittee arises from exactly $n!$ orderings, so the number of subcommittees is $\dfrac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-n+1)}{n!}=\binom zn$. If $n>z$ the product contains the factor $z-z=0$, matching the fact that there are no such subcommittees; for $n=0$, $z\ge1$ the single (empty) subcommittee corresponds to $\binom z0=1$; for $z=0$, $n\ge1$, the product has the factor $0$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-03.title: Counting and negative arguments
dmm-2007-power-03.body:
$\binom xn$ is a polynomial in $x$ with rational coefficients (degree $n$). For an integer $z\ge0$ the previous result says $\binom zn$ is the number of subcommittees, so it is a (nonnegative) integer. For a negative integer $z=-w$ ($w\ge1$):
$$z(z-1)\cdots(z-n+1)=(-1)^n\,w(w+1)\cdots(w+n-1),$$
so $\binom zn=(-1)^n\dfrac{w(w+1)\cdots(w+n-1)}{n!}=(-1)^n\dbinom{w+n-1}{n}$, which is again an integer by the counting interpretation. So $\binom zn\in\mathbb Z$ for all integers $z$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-04.title: Legendre's formula and a counting argument
dmm-2007-power-04.body:
**The power in $n!$.** Among $1,\dots,n$ exactly $\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor$ numbers are divisible by $p^i$. Since the exponent of $p$ in $m$ is the number of $i\ge1$ with $p^i\mid m$, the exponent of $p$ in $n!$ is $v=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac n{p^i}\right\rfloor$ (a finite sum), i.e. the largest power is $p^v$.

**The product of consecutive integers.** Any $p^i$ consecutive integers contain exactly one multiple of $p^i$. Split $x_1,\dots,x_n$ into $\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor$ disjoint blocks of $p^i$ consecutive integers; each contains a multiple of $p^i$, so at least $\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor$ of the $x_j$ are divisible by $p^i$. By the same counting as above, the exponent of $p$ in $x_1\cdots x_n$ is $\sum_{i\ge1}\#\{j: p^i\mid x_j\}\ge\sum_i\lfloor n/p^i\rfloor=v$. So $p^v\mid x_1x_2\cdots x_n$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-05.title: Divisibility by $n!$
dmm-2007-power-05.body: For an integer $z$, the numerator $z(z-1)\cdots(z-n+1)$ is a product of $n$ consecutive integers. By the previous result it is divisible by the full power of every prime $p\le n$ appearing in $n!$ (primes $>n$ do not divide $n!$). Hence $n!$ divides the numerator and $\binom zn$ is an integer. ∎

dmm-2007-power-06.title: Closure
dmm-2007-power-06.body: Each $\binom xk$ is an integer-valued polynomial, so for every integer $z$ each $a_k\binom zk$ is an integer (integer times integer), and a finite sum of integers is an integer. A finite sum of polynomials is a polynomial. ∎

dmm-2007-power-09.title: Direct
dmm-2007-power-09.body: If $f$ is a polynomial, so is $x\mapsto f(x+1)$ (expand the powers), and the difference of two polynomials is a polynomial. If $f$ is integer-valued and $z\in\mathbb Z$, then $f(z+1)$ and $f(z)$ are integers, so $(\Delta f)(z)$ is an integer. ∎

dmm-2007-power-10.title: Infinitely many roots
dmm-2007-power-10.body: $\Delta f=0$ means $f(x+1)=f(x)$ for all $x$, so $f(0)=f(1)=f(2)=\cdots=c$. The polynomial $f(x)-c$ has infinitely many roots, so it is the zero polynomial and $f\equiv c$. If $f$ is integer-valued, $c=f(0)\in\mathbb Z$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-11.title: Subtract
dmm-2007-power-11.body: By linearity, $\Delta(f-g)=\Delta f-\Delta g=0$, and $f-g$ is a polynomial, so by the previous result $f-g=C$ is constant. If $f,g$ are integer-valued, so is $f-g$, and then $C=f(0)-g(0)\in\mathbb Z$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-12.title: Binomial theorem
dmm-2007-power-12.body: By linearity, $\Delta f=\sum_{k=0}^nc_k\bigl((x+1)^k-x^k\bigr)$. By the binomial theorem $(x+1)^k-x^k=kx^{k-1}+\binom k2x^{k-2}+\cdots+1$ has degree exactly $k-1$ for $k\ge1$ and is $0$ for $k=0$. For $k<n$ these terms have degree $\le n-2$. So the $x^{n-1}$ coefficient of $\Delta f$ comes only from $k=n$ and equals $nc_n\ne0$, and no higher power occurs. Hence $\deg\Delta f=n-1$ with leading term $nc_nx^{n-1}$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-13.title: Factor out the common product
dmm-2007-power-13.body:
$\binom{x+1}{n+1}-\binom x{n+1}=\dfrac{(x+1)x(x-1)\cdots(x-n+1)-x(x-1)\cdots(x-n+1)(x-n)}{(n+1)!}=\dfrac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-n+1)\,[(x+1)-(x-n)]}{(n+1)!}=\dfrac{(n+1)\,x(x-1)\cdots(x-n+1)}{(n+1)!}=\binom xn.$$
(For $n=0$ the product is empty and the formula reads $(x+1)-x=1=\binom x0$.) ∎

dmm-2007-power-14.title: Constants
dmm-2007-power-14.body: A constant integer-valued polynomial equals $c=f(0)\in\mathbb Z$, and $f=c\binom x0$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-15.title: Induction step
dmm-2007-power-15.body: $f$ has degree $k+1\ge1$, so $\Delta f$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ (previous problem) which is integer-valued. By hypothesis $\Delta f=\sum_{j=0}^ka_j\binom xj$ with integers $a_j$. Let $g(x)=\sum_{j=0}^ka_j\binom x{j+1}$, an integer linear combination of binomial coefficients, hence an integer-valued polynomial. By linearity and $\Delta\binom x{j+1}=\binom xj$ we get $\Delta g=\sum a_j\binom xj=\Delta f$. So $f=g+C$ with $C\in\mathbb Z$ (both integer-valued), i.e. $f=\sum a_j\binom x{j+1}+C\binom x0$, an integer linear combination of binomial coefficients. ∎

dmm-2007-power-16.title: Induction
dmm-2007-power-16.body: Let $S(k)$ be the statement "every integer-valued polynomial of degree $k$ is an integer linear combination of binomial coefficients". $S(0)$ holds by the first fact, and $S(k)\Rightarrow S(k+1)$ by the second. By induction $S(k)$ holds for all $k\ge0$, so every integer-valued polynomial of degree $\ge0$ is such a combination (the zero polynomial is the combination with all $a_i=0$). ∎

dmm-2007-power-17.title: Periodic function
dmm-2007-power-17.body: $g(x)=\sin(2\pi x)$ has period $1$, so $g(x+1)=g(x)$ and $\Delta g=0$, but $g$ is not constant (and not a polynomial). Another example: $g(x)=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$.

dmm-2007-power-19.title: Newton's forward difference formula
dmm-2007-power-19.body:
**Algorithm.** Let $d=\deg f$. Compute $f(0),f(1),\dots,f(d)$, then $a_k=(\Delta^kf)(0)=\sum_{j=0}^k(-1)^{k-j}\binom kjf(j)$ for $k=0,\dots,d$ (a difference table). If every $a_k$ is an integer, $f$ is integer-valued and $f=\sum_{k=0}^da_k\binom xk$ with $m=d$ (and $a_m=d!\,c_d\ne0$); otherwise $f$ is not integer-valued.

**Why it works.** Let $E f(x)=f(x+1)$, so $E=1+\Delta$ and $E^j=\sum_k\binom jk\Delta^k$ (binomial theorem for commuting operators). Hence for integer $j\ge0$: $f(j)=(E^jf)(0)=\sum_{k=0}^j\binom jk(\Delta^kf)(0)=\sum_{k=0}^d\binom jka_k$ (terms with $k>d$ vanish since $\Delta^kf=0$ for $k>d$, by the degree-lowering fact; also $\binom jk=0$ for $k>j$). So $f$ and $g=\sum_{k=0}^da_k\binom xk$ are polynomials of degree $\le d$ agreeing at $x=0,1,\dots,d$ ($d+1$ points), so $f=g$.

If all $a_k\in\mathbb Z$, $f$ is an integer linear combination of binomial coefficients and so integer-valued (Part 1). Conversely if $f$ is integer-valued, each $a_k$ is an integer combination of the integers $f(0),\dots,f(k)$. By the uniqueness result the representation is the only one, with $m=d$ since $\deg\binom xk=k$ and $a_d=d!\,c_d\ne0$. ∎

dmm-2007-power-20a.title: Test with the difference table
dmm-2007-power-20a.body: The values at $x=0,1,2,3,4,5$ are $0,0,\frac15,1,3,7$; the Newton coefficients are $a_0=0,a_1=0,a_2=\frac15,a_3=\frac25,a_4=\frac15,a_5=0$ (not all integers). Indeed at $x=2$ the value is $\frac{1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4}{120}=\frac15\notin\mathbb Z$. So the polynomial is **not** integer-valued.

dmm-2007-power-20b.title: Newton coefficients
dmm-2007-power-20b.body:
This polynomial is $\binom{x+2}5$, so it is integer-valued (Vandermonde: $\binom{x+2}{5}=\binom x5+2\binom x4+\binom x3$). Via the difference table: values at $x=0,\dots,5$ are $0,0,0,1,6,21$, so $a_0=a_1=a_2=0$, $a_3=1$, $a_4=6-4\cdot1=2$, $a_5=21-5\cdot6+10\cdot1=1$.

**Answer:** $\binom x3+2\binom x4+\binom x5$.

dmm-2007-power-20c.title: Newton coefficients
dmm-2007-power-20c.body:
The values at $x=0,1,2,3,4,5$ are $0,3,12,30,64,133$. Differences: $\Delta f(0)=3$; $\Delta^2f(0)=12-6=6$; $\Delta^3f(0)=30-36+9=3$; $\Delta^4f(0)=64-120+72-12=4$; $\Delta^5f(0)=133-320+300-120+15=8$ (using $a_k=\sum(-1)^{k-j}\binom kjf(j)$). All are integers, so $f$ is integer-valued and
$$f=3\binom x1+6\binom x2+3\binom x3+4\binom x4+8\binom x5.$$

dmm-2007-power-20d.title: Newton coefficients
dmm-2007-power-20d.body:
Values at $x=0,\dots,5$: $0,1,32,243,1024,3125$. The Newton coefficients $\Delta^kf(0)$ are $0,1,30,150,240,120$ (note $\Delta^5x^5=5!=120$). So
$$x^5=\binom x1+30\binom x2+150\binom x3+240\binom x4+120\binom x5.$$
(These are $k!\,S(5,k)$ with $S$ the Stirling numbers of the second kind.)
